Mathematics examples

46 programs, each reproducing a published or classical result by computation. Exact finite constructions, bilinear/polynomial identity certificates, finite formal expansions and numerical comparisons have different scopes, stated per entry under Arithmetic and Limits.

Every one of these 46 programs was run at release SHA 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release build, macOS arm64, measured 2026-10-09) in native JIT and native AOT. 46 completed in both modes; 45 of those printed their own verdict RESULT: ALL PASS with Failed: 0 in both modes, and the other 1 prints diagnostics or a receipt without a RESULT: line (status RAN-OK: exit 0, no runtime-error line; the entry quotes the output). Wall times measured with 6 programs running concurrently on a shared machine; CPU user/sys from wait4.

Each entry gives: the published result being reproduced and its references; what the program computes and by which algorithm; the domain and parameters; the arithmetic and its scope; the checks the source asserts; the honest limits; and the measured outcome at the release SHA with the computed values that matter, quoted verbatim from the program’s output. A reference marked as cited in the program’s source comments is taken from the program header; (citation unverified) marks one whose bibliographic details could not be confirmed.

Abelian sheaves on finite sites

Source: mathematics_abelian_sheaves_finite_site.esk. SHA-256: 1b516d970bf01f9ae7f7e65232bac390a8804c17b8034ba59ff3528978a70136.

Published result: On a finite T₀ space (Alexandrov topology), sheaves are the same as presheaves on the poset of points (McCord); sheafification a = (−)⁺⁺ is exact and left adjoint to the inclusion (Mac Lane–Moerdijk III.5); and sheaf cohomology equals the derived functors of the limit over the points, which Čech cohomology of a cover computes when the cover is Leray (Bredon III.4). The program computes all three statements over Q on the pseudocircle (the 4-point model of S¹) and the pseudo-2-sphere (the 6-point model of S²), including the case where the Leray hypothesis fails.

References:

  • M. C. McCord, “Singular homology groups and homotopy groups of finite topological spaces”, Duke Math. J. 33 (1966). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • S. Mac Lane, I. Moerdijk, Sheaves in Geometry and Logic, Springer (1992). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • A. K. Bousfield, D. M. Kan, Homotopy Limits, Completions and Localizations, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 304, Springer (1972). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • G. E. Bredon, Sheaf Theory, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 170, Springer (1997). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • C. A. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, Cambridge University Press (1994). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Compare sheafification and cohomology routes on finite Alexandrov sites.

Implemented algorithm: Build rational restriction matrices, matching-family kernels, plus construction, pointwise limits and Cech/derived-limit complexes.

Domain and parameters: Pseudocircle and pseudo-2-sphere; constant Q, a nonseparated presheaf and a monodromy -1 local system.

Arithmetic: Exact rational linear algebra and kernel/rank computations over Q.

Checks in the source: Functor laws, separated/sheaf conditions, point-route dimensions and kernel/cokernel dimensions are checked; the sphere cover deliberately misses H² when it is not Leray.

Limits: Rational coefficients omit torsion. Dimensionwise checks of exactness/comparison must not be described as a machine proof of the general sheafification theorem.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Measured at 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release, macOS arm64): native JIT PASS (Passed: 8, Failed: 0; 7.98 s); native AOT PASS (Passed: 8, Failed: 0; compile 40.4 s, run 0.50 s). CTest: cat_abelian_sheaves_finite_site_jit Passed (40.9 s), cat_abelian_sheaves_finite_site_aot Passed (40.0 s). Verdict line: RESULT: ALL PASS.

Rank-23 matrix multiplication over F₂

Source: mathematics_alphatensor_3x3_gf2.esk. SHA-256: 7f439ceb1a3ea82e8a500f5421320f53963909e2198cc3f358dd81fbd51ffdd5.

Published result: Fawzi et al. (Nature, 2022) used reinforcement learning (AlphaTensor) to search for low-rank decompositions of matrix-multiplication tensors and published the decompositions they found. For 3×3 matrices the rank 23 they report over F₂ equals Laderman’s 1976 bound; the program checks the public rank-23 factor matrices from the AlphaTensor repository, not a new bound.

References:

  • A. Fawzi, M. Balog, A. Huang et al., “Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning”, Nature 610, 47–53 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05172-4
  • google-deepmind/alphatensor: published factorizations. https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphatensor (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Verify a supplied public AlphaTensor factorization.

Implemented algorithm: Contract U/V/W integer bit masks by parity of bitwise intersections.

Domain and parameters: 3×3 matrices over F₂; all 9×9 pairs of matrix units; fixed rank 23 witness.

Arithmetic: Exact integers and reduction modulo 2.

Checks in the source: Basis-pair expansion agrees with matrix-unit multiplication; bilinearity extends this complete tensor identity to every pair of 3×3 F₂ matrices. How the verdict is read: the program prints one PASS:/FAIL: line per check, Passed:/Failed: counts and a final RESULT: ALL PASS or RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED; the verdict is the program’s RESULT: line, and the measurements below read it. The process also exits 0 on RESULT: ALL PASS and 1 on RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED, so a failing check is a nonzero exit as well as a printed line.

Limits: Certifies the supplied bilinear witness over F₂; does not search for it or prove rank optimality.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Measured at 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release, macOS arm64): native JIT PASS (Passed: 2, Failed: 0; 2.04 s); native AOT PASS (Passed: 2, Failed: 0; compile 1.98 s, run 0.23 s). CTest: alphatensor_rank23_gf2_jit Passed (0.24 s), alphatensor_rank23_gf2_aot Passed (2.22 s). Verdict line: RESULT: ALL PASS.

Computed values (verbatim program output):

PASS: rank-23 factorization has 23 bilinear products
PASS: rank-23 tensor expands to 3x3 multiplication over F2
Basis pairs checked: 81

Rank-47 matrix multiplication over F₂

Source: mathematics_alphatensor_gf2.esk. SHA-256: 97b4bebee4eba04141d1618cfac8fdada8ca1de719d26f7b36dc10ce150a5940.

Published result: Fawzi et al. (Nature, 2022) report a rank-47 decomposition of the 4×4 matrix-multiplication tensor over F₂, below the rank 49 obtained by applying Strassen’s 2×2 algorithm recursively — the first improvement on that bound for 4×4 matrices over a finite field. The program checks the published rank-47 factor matrices.

References:

  • A. Fawzi, M. Balog, A. Huang et al., “Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning”, Nature 610, 47–53 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05172-4
  • google-deepmind/alphatensor: published factorizations. https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphatensor (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Verify the supplied 4×4 AlphaTensor factorization.

Implemented algorithm: Contract the fixed rank-47 U/V/W bit-mask factors and compare with ordinary matrix multiplication.

Domain and parameters: 4×4 matrices over F₂; all 16×16 matrix-unit pairs plus a nontrivial sample.

Arithmetic: Exact integer bitsets with parity reduction.

Checks in the source: The complete basis expansion certifies the bilinear multiplication tensor for all inputs over F₂. How the verdict is read: the program prints one PASS:/FAIL: line per check, Passed:/Failed: counts and a final RESULT: ALL PASS or RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED; the verdict is the program’s RESULT: line, and the measurements below read it. The process also exits 0 on RESULT: ALL PASS and 1 on RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED, so a failing check is a nonzero exit as well as a printed line.

Limits: No factorization search, field-independent rank claim, or rank-optimality proof is implemented.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Measured at 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release, macOS arm64): native JIT PASS (Passed: 3, Failed: 0; 2.32 s); native AOT PASS (Passed: 3, Failed: 0; compile 2.85 s, run 0.42 s). CTest: alphatensor_rank47_gf2_jit Passed (0.56 s), alphatensor_rank47_gf2_aot Passed (2.75 s). Verdict line: RESULT: ALL PASS.

Computed values (verbatim program output):

Cycle supports on the Fermat sextic surface

Source: mathematics_aoki_cycles_fermat_sextic.esk. SHA-256: 2367ee5fcc98cde07590fce5085459b276442f35518dfc46e675ed720591b28e.

Published result: On the Fermat sextic surface X₆² ⊂ P³ the Picard number is 86 (85 primitive Hodge characters plus the hyperplane class). Shioda (1979) shows the 108 lines span only the 62-dimensional part carried by the 61 ‘standard’ characters; Aoki (1987) constructs further curves (for p = 2 and p = 3) to reach the remaining characters, and Villaflor Loyola’s period formula (Manuscripta Math.) identifies the primitive class of a complete-intersection curve with the class of a Jacobian determinant in the Griffiths Jacobian ring. The program computes, by that formula, the character support of each family and reports how many of the 85 nontrivial Hodge characters the lines and Aoki’s two curve families cover together.

References:

  • R. Villaflor Loyola, “Periods of complete intersection algebraic cycles”, Manuscripta Math. (published online 2021; the program header gives 2022), arXiv:1812.03964. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00229-021-01290-x
  • T. Shioda, “The Hodge conjecture for Fermat varieties”, Math. Ann. 245 (1979). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • N. Aoki, J. Math. Soc. Japan 39 (1987): Theorem 1-1 (lines), Remark 2-2 and Theorem 2-1 (the p = 2 and p = 3 curves). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • N. Aoki, T. Shioda, “Generators of the Néron-Severi group of a Fermat surface” (1983). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • P. A. Griffiths, “On the periods of certain rational integrals”, Ann. of Math. 90 (1969). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Measure which rational Hodge characters the supplied lines and two Aoki curve families cover.

Implemented algorithm: Expand sparse four-variable factorizations and Jacobian determinants in the exact extension tower; reduce in the Jacobian ring and close supports under permutations/Galois actions.

Domain and parameters: Degree-6 surface X₆²; lines, p=2,d=3 curve C and p=3,d=2 curve Y; 85 primitive Hodge characters.

Arithmetic: Exact Q(ζ₁₂)[c]/(c³−2) coefficients and integer exponents.

Checks in the source: Tower relations, polynomial decompositions, line supports, Galois closure and Hodge membership are asserted; a receipt records the uncovered support count.

Limits: A PASS receipt reports the computed gap for its parameters; it does not imply the gap is zero. Period and support conclusions use the cited geometric results.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Measured at 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release, macOS arm64): native JIT PASS (Passed: 8, Failed: 0; 5.68 s); native AOT PASS (Passed: 8, Failed: 0; compile 14.9 s, run 0.26 s). CTest: hodge_aoki_cycles_fermat_sextic_jit Passed (11.2 s), hodge_aoki_cycles_fermat_sextic_aot Passed (11.7 s). Verdict line: RESULT: ALL PASS.

Computed values (verbatim program output):

PASS: Shioda's Theorem 1-1 as a computation: the support of [L] is exactly the 25 characters with a_0 + a_1 = a_2 + a_3 = 0 mod 6
PASS: all lines together: the 61 standard characters (those with a zero-sum pair), so the lines span 62 of 86 Hodge classes as in the Gram computation
  support of Aoki's curve C: count, Galois-closed, all Hodge = (4 #t #t)
  support of Aoki's curve Y (p = 3): count, Galois-closed, all Hodge = (6 #t #t)
  characters covered by lines, permutations of C, permutations of Y; missing Hodge characters = (61 24 12 85 0)
GAP 0

Aoki cycle supports by surface degree

Source: mathematics_aoki_cycles_fermat_surfaces_sweep.esk. SHA-256: 33d0a77acceb97ce29a75d0a70f659cd53c118e7d9c8d503094d257f6c77e56f.

Published result: Aoki proves that for prime-power degree m the p-standard cycles (lines and his curve families) generate the Néron–Severi group of the Fermat surface X_m² over Q; for composite m his Theorem 1-3 also needs ‘semi-standard’ elements for which explicit subvarieties are known only in a few cases. The program measures the residual exactly for one chosen degree: the number of Hodge characters left uncovered by the supports of the lines and of the available curve families, each support computed from the Jacobian determinant of Villaflor Loyola’s period formula.

References:

  • R. Villaflor Loyola, “Periods of complete intersection algebraic cycles”, Manuscripta Math. (published online 2021; the program header gives 2022), arXiv:1812.03964. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00229-021-01290-x
  • N. Aoki, J. Math. Soc. Japan 39 (1987): Theorem 1-1 (lines), Remark 2-2 and Theorem 2-1 (the p = 2 and p = 3 curves). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • T. Shioda, “The Hodge conjecture for Fermat varieties”, Math. Ann. 245 (1979). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • P. A. Griffiths, “On the periods of certain rational integrals”, Ann. of Math. 90 (1969). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Sweep the supports of available p-standard cycles against Fermat-surface Hodge characters.

Implemented algorithm: Construct degree-dependent cyclotomic/radical towers, verify polynomial decompositions and union line/C/Y/Q supports across divisor levels; organize residual character orbits and bounded multiset witnesses.

Domain and parameters: MATH_FERMAT_DEGREE defaults 8 (header domain m≥4); eligible C levels are even, Y levels divisible by 3 and Q levels divisible by 4; MATH_WITNESS_K defaults 4.

Arithmetic: Exact sparse polynomial and extension-field arithmetic.

Checks in the source: JSON receipt reports C/Y/Q support and cover counts, divisor levels, missing characters/orbits, bounded inductive witnesses and no-witness counts; PASS checks support/Hodge/Galois consistency, not zero missing count.

Limits: The Q-family decomposition is checked as an exact polynomial identity; the earlier modular screen was a discovery method. The bounded witness search reports no witness only within its configured bound, which does not imply that no algebraic cycle exists.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Measured at 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release, macOS arm64): native JIT PASS (7.12 s); native AOT PASS (compile 28.2 s, run 0.27 s). CTest: hodge_aoki_surface_sweep_default_jit Passed (32.7 s), hodge_aoki_surface_sweep_default_aot Passed (27.5 s). Verdict line: RESULT: ALL PASS.

Finite-group classifying spaces and state sums

Source: mathematics_classifying_space_dijkgraaf_witten.esk. SHA-256: 8f88b7dec7f8bc1362bd3c5b9d082a9c21b3c3ce5a5e99f90436a607ded6e172.

Published result: Dijkgraaf and Witten (1990) define a topological gauge theory for a finite group G twisted by a class ω ∈ H³(BG; U(1)) ≅ H³(BG; Q/Z), and give its partition function on a closed oriented 3-manifold as a state sum over flat G-connections weighted by ω evaluated on the tetrahedra; untwisted, Z(M) = |Hom(π₁M, G)|/|G|. The program computes the chain from the nerve of G (the bar construction, a model of BG) through integral homology and the twists to the state sums on S³, RP³ and T³, and checks each value against the closed formulas.

References:

  • R. Dijkgraaf, E. Witten, “Topological gauge theories and group cohomology”, Comm. Math. Phys. 129 (1990). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press (2002). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • K. S. Brown, Cohomology of Groups, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 87, Springer (1982). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Connect explicit bar-complex homology, Q/Z cocycles and Dijkgraaf–Witten state sums.

Implemented algorithm: Build nerve boundary matrices and integer Smith forms; test cocycles/coboundaries, enumerate flat colorings of branched Delta-complexes and pair cocycles with fundamental cycles.

Domain and parameters: Z/2, Z/3, (Z/2)² and S₃ homology cases; state sums on the supplied S³, RP³ and T³ complexes with the implemented groups/twists.

Arithmetic: Exact bignum integer linear algebra, rational cocycles modulo 1 and exact sign phases.

Checks in the source: Homology and twist counts, untwisted connection counts, lens/commuting-triple formulas, RP³ fundamental-class pairing and a wrong-orientation negative control are checked.

Limits: Finite supplied complexes and group/twist sets delimit the computation; no universal classification of arbitrary manifolds or gauge groups is executed.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Measured at 60f345def (Eshkol Compiler v1.3.6-evolve, Release, macOS arm64): native JIT PASS (Passed: 40, Failed: 0; 6.39 s); native AOT PASS (Passed: 40, Failed: 0; compile 13.8 s, run 1.16 s). CTest: dw_classifying_space_state_sums_jit Passed (15.1 s), dw_classifying_space_state_sums_aot Passed (14.5 s). Verdict line: RESULT: ALL PASS.

Published result: By Milnor (1958) and Whitehead (1949) the homotopy type of a simply connected closed 4-manifold is determined by its intersection form. S²×S² (even form) and CP²#CP² (odd form) have the same homology and the same 2-type K(Z², 2); the difference is Wu’s class, the parity of the form. Published result: Cohomological descent (Deligne, Théorie de Hodge III, §5.3): for any cover, the total complex of the Čech–sheaf double complex computes sheaf cohomology, whereas plain Čech cohomology does so only for a Leray cover. Hypercohomology of a complex of sheaves is invariant under quasi-isomorphism (Weibel §5.7). Source: mathematics_fermat_hodge_classes_sweep.esk. SHA-256: 25ba69494aaef6f87f64ade1c0f8861aa7cbdd32a01aace3ed34c40c3d2470c4.

Published result: For the Fermat variety X_m^n of even dimension n, the primitive Hodge numbers follow from Griffiths’ Jacobian ring and, independently, from Shioda’s character decomposition (1979); the rational Hodge classes are the Galois-closed characters of type (n/2, n/2) plus the power of the hyperplane class. Shioda’s Theorem I shows the Hodge classes are algebraic when every Hodge character contains a pair aᵢ + aⱼ ≡ 0 (mod m). The program writes, for one (m, n), the Hodge dimension and the rank modulo a prime of the intersection matrix of the linear cycles xᵢ = ζxⱼ.

References:

  • P. A. Griffiths, “On the periods of certain rational integrals”, Ann. of Math. 90 (1969). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • T. Shioda, “The Hodge conjecture for Fermat varieties”, Math. Ann. 245 (1979). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • N. Aoki, T. Shioda, “Generators of the Néron-Severi group of a Fermat surface” (1983). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • W. Fulton, Intersection Theory, §6.3 (excess intersection). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Compare Hodge dimensions with the span detected by the linear-cycle intersection matrix.

Implemented algorithm: Count Jacobian-ring monomials and Galois-closed characters; enumerate coordinate matchings/cycles; build exact intersection numbers and eliminate modulo a prime.

Domain and parameters: MATH_FERMAT_DEGREE m≥3 (default 4), MATH_FERMAT_DIM even 2 or 4 (default 2), MATH_FERMAT_PRIME prime (default 10007).

Arithmetic: Exact integer counts/intersections and finite-field matrix rank.

Checks in the source: Receipt compares Griffiths/Shioda counts, nonnegative gap and the modular rank against the Hodge dimension.

Limits: Rank modulo p lower-bounds rational rank. A zero gap together with the stated geometric upper bound certifies spanning for that parameter case; a positive gap only bounds the missing dimension and is not an exact rational-rank result. The conclusion depends on valid parameters and the cited geometric formulas.

Sheaf cohomology of finite spaces

Source: mathematics_finite_spaces_sheaf_cohomology.esk. SHA-256: 53c55836b821e593f8749f058b67ab43f93b6f25fde7b64e0f92569ff60bfcc1.

Published result: McCord (1966): a finite T₀ space is weakly equivalent to the order complex of its poset, so the pseudocircle (4 points) and the pseudo-2-sphere (6 points) have the cohomology of S¹ and S². Sheaf cohomology on a finite space is the derived limit over the poset (Bousfield–Kan XI.6–7), and Čech cohomology computes it on a Leray cover (Bredon III.4). The program computes these with integer coefficients, so torsion from local systems (monodromy −1) is visible.

References:

  • M. C. McCord, “Singular homology groups and homotopy groups of finite topological spaces”, Duke Math. J. 33 (1966). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

  • G. E. Bredon, Sheaf Theory, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 170, Springer (1997). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Compute derived limits and compare Leray-cover Cech descent while retaining torsion.

Arithmetic: Exact integer matrices/Smith normal forms.

Checks in the source: Functor laws, differential squares, constant/twisted groups and Leray Cech agreement are asserted; a partial cover gives the wrong H¹ as a negative control.

Limits: The comparisons apply to the listed finite models and coefficient systems; non-Leray covers require the separate descent construction.

Source: mathematics_four_manifolds_second_k_invariant.esk. SHA-256: f895a42c6c178071c3fdc8cd578d71edb713f78ce40e1e11f261071be010f69d.

Published result: Serre (1953): H*(K(Z/2, n); Z/2) is polynomial on admissible Steenrod squares; in particular Sq²ι₂ = ι₂ ∪ ι₂ spans H⁴(K(Z/2, 2); Z/2), so the 3-type with π₂ = π₃ = Z/2 and k-invariant ι∪ι exists. A map X → P lifts a class x ∈ H²(X; Z/2) exactly when x∪x = 0 (Hatcher §4.3), so on a 4-manifold the second k-invariant sees the intersection form mod 2. The program computes the mapping-space cardinality by a cochain state sum and by the Postnikov fibration formula on S⁴, RP⁴ and S²×S².

Source: mathematics_funsearch_cap_set.esk. SHA-256: 45d91a4f2f3503bb752ee024d6dca7e50eb8e3fb2fe66cd46e598fbfe6b600a6.

Published result: Romera-Paredes et al. (Nature, 2024) used FunSearch — an LLM-guided evolutionary search over programs — to find a cap set of size 512 in F₃⁸ (AG(8,3)), larger than the previously best known 496. A cap set has no three collinear points (no x, y, z distinct with x + y + z ≡ 0). The program rebuilds the published 512-point witness from its explicit construction and checks the cap property exhaustively.

References:

  • B. Romera-Paredes, M. Barekatain, A. Novikov et al., “Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models”, Nature 625, 468–475 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06924-6
  • google-deepmind/funsearch: published cap-set witnesses. https://github.com/google-deepmind/funsearch (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Verify a supplied public cap-set construction.

Implemented algorithm: Enumerate 3⁸ vectors, select the construction classes and test the third point on every affine line determined by an unordered cap-point pair.

Domain and parameters: AG(8,3); fixed construction with 512 points and 130816 unordered pairs.

Arithmetic: Exact integer coordinates modulo 3.

Checks in the source: Ambient and cap cardinalities and exhaustive absence of a third cap point establish the finite no-three-collinear property. How the verdict is read: the program prints one PASS:/FAIL: line per check, Passed:/Failed: counts and a final RESULT: ALL PASS or RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED; the verdict is the program’s RESULT: line, and the measurements below read it. The process also exits 0 on RESULT: ALL PASS and 1 on RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED, so a failing check is a nonzero exit as well as a printed line.

Limits: This certifies the supplied set; it neither reruns FunSearch nor proves a maximum cap size.

Published result: For the Fermat quartic fourfold X₄⁴ ⊂ P⁵, Shioda’s Theorem I (Math. Ann. 245, 1979) implies that every rational Hodge class is algebraic, because every Hodge character contains a pair aᵢ + aⱼ ≡ 0 (mod 4). The program makes this explicit: it computes the Hodge numbers twice (Griffiths’ Jacobian ring and Shioda’s characters), enumerates the 960 planes on X, computes their 960×960 intersection matrix from excess-intersection numbers, and shows its rank is 142 = dim of the space of rational Hodge classes, so the planes span every Hodge class. It repeats the line computation on the Fermat quartic, quintic and sextic surfaces.

Polynomial Jacobian map and fibers

Source: mathematics_jacobian_counterexample.esk. SHA-256: 17695cfcfb489d40a4e842192c87e55dc218de708bad7bf380618eae1a2a0238.

Published result: The research note “A counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture” (dated July 20, 2026) verifies that the polynomial map F = (P, Q, R): C³ → C³ with P = (1+xy)³z + y²(1+xy)(4+3xy), Q = y + 3x(1+xy)²z + 3xy²(4+3xy), R = 2x − 3x²y − x³z has det Jac F ≡ −2 (a Keller map) and that F(0, 0, −1/4) = F(1, −3/2, 13/2) = F(−1, 3/2, 13/2) = (−1/4, 0, 0) (Theorem 3.1), so F is not injective and hence not a polynomial automorphism; by stabilization this gives counterexamples in every dimension n ≥ 3. The note credits the explicit formula to an announcement by L. Alpöge. Theorem 5.1 gives a family F_{λ,a,c,H} with the same mechanism. The program checks the map, the three-point fiber, the binary-cubic fiber description, the discriminant fiber counts, the determinant identity and two members of the Theorem 5.1 family.

References:

  • “A counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture”, research note dated July 20, 2026 (the extracted PDF text carries no author line). https://www.ulam.ai/research/jacobian.pdf
  • O.-H. Keller, “Ganze Cremona-Transformationen”, Monatsh. Math. Phys. 47 (1939) (the conjecture), as cited by the note.
  • H. Bass, E. H. Connell, D. Wright, “The Jacobian conjecture: reduction of degree and formal expansion of the inverse”, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 7 (1982), as cited by the note. https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1982-15032-7

Purpose: Verify the explicit map, finite fibers and determinant identities supplied by the cited paper.

Implemented algorithm: Compute P,Q,R and cubic/discriminant fiber data; use reverse AD through a closure factory and independent explicit partials on an exact degree grid.

Domain and parameters: Three rational preimages of (-1/4,0,0); a 9×8×3 determinant grid with coordinate degree bounds (8,7,2); two Theorem-5.1 parameter cases.

Arithmetic: Exact rational polynomial/fiber checks; AD carrier checks use tolerance 1e-9, including rational-input vectors.

Checks in the source: The over-degree grid certifies the polynomial determinant identity globally, while the AD comparisons remain numerical. The supplied rational preimages are checked explicitly. How the verdict is read: the program prints one PASS:/FAIL: line per check, Passed:/Failed: counts and a final RESULT: ALL PASS or RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED; the verdict is the program’s RESULT: line, and the measurements below read it. The process also exits 0 on RESULT: ALL PASS and 1 on RESULT: FAILURES DETECTED, so a failing check is a nonzero exit as well as a printed line.

Limits: The exact degree-grid determinant certificate and tolerance-based AD comparisons have different scopes. Interpreting the construction as a real or complex Jacobian conjecture counterexample depends on the paper’s domain and hypotheses.

Published result: A simplicial set is a Kan complex when every horn has a filler (Kan 1958); it is a quasi-category when every inner horn does, and a quasi-category is Kan exactly when it is a groupoid (Joyal 2002). The nerve of a 2-groupoid has unique fillers for horns of dimension ≥ 3 (Duskin 2002), and Kan’s combinatorial homotopy groups of the nerve of a crossed module M → N are π₁ = coker and π₂ = ker. The program counts horns and fillers on four 2-group nerves and on the nerve of the pseudocircle poset.

Published result: Reidemeister (1935) and Franz (1935) classified lens spaces up to homeomorphism by torsion: L(p, q) ≅ L(p, q′) iff q′ ≡ ±q^{±1} (mod p), and τ(L(p, q)) = (ζ − 1)(ζ^r − 1) up to ±ζ^k with rq ≡ 1 (mod p) (Milnor, Whitehead torsion §12; Turaev, Thm. 2.2 and §10). L(7, 1) and L(7, 2) are homotopy equivalent but not homeomorphic — the classical example that torsion sees and homotopy invariants cannot. The program computes τ in Q(ζ_p) for seven lens complexes.

Published result: Whitehead (1941): L(p, q) and L(p, q′) are homotopy equivalent iff qq′ is a square mod p, detected by the square class of the linking pairing ⟨x ∪ βx, [L]⟩. Yetter’s invariant for a 2-group is the homotopy cardinality of the mapping space into its classifying space (Faria Martins–Porter 2007), so a nonzero k-invariant can obstruct lifts. The program computes the lens complexes’ cohomology and Whitehead’s square class, and Yetter’s invariants for an order-three k-invariant, by a reduced state sum and by the Postnikov fibration formula.

Cutoffs, periodization and discrete energy

Source: mathematics_navier_stokes_localization.esk. SHA-256: 3f42a5ad891e010417e6625ce2921181eefcdfabdfdc72b765f7b70cdbe768ff.

Published result: Section 10 of the reference construction (Proposition 10.1, Lemmas 10.2–10.4, (10.20)–(10.23), Corollary 10.6): the local solution is multiplied by smooth cutoffs to give a compactly supported force, the energy identity holds with the force defined as the residual, and compact support transports the construction to the torus T³ = R³/Z³. The program checks four ingredients: a cutoff that cancels a temporal pole, exact compact support, periodization within one cell, and the discrete energy identity.

References:

  • OpenAI, “Finite time blowup for Navier–Stokes” (2026; the PDF carries no date line, the year is the one the program headers give). Theorem 1.1 constructs, for every viscosity ν > 0, a smooth force compactly supported in space and time and a smooth solution of the forced incompressible equations, starting from rest, whose kinetic energy stays bounded while its velocity becomes unbounded as t ↑ 1. https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/32d9f210-8b73-45e0-91bc-82a30aef8a9a/navier-stokes.pdf

Purpose: Check localization ingredients in explicitly constructed fields.

Implemented algorithm: Cancel a temporal pole with a cutoff polynomial, guard spatial bumps, periodize within one cell and differentiate a discrete energy model.

Domain and parameters: Source-defined support boxes/radii and period cell; three registered criteria for smooth extension, energy and torus scaling.

Arithmetic: Rational finite-grid/cutoff data and AD; the discrete energy equality is asserted exactly.

Checks in the source: Support/period-cell agreement, torus averages, exact energy balance and oversized-radius/dropped-viscosity negative controls are asserted.

Limits: Checks the stated finite model of one step of the reference construction; it does not reproduce the construction’s analytic estimates, and nothing here is a machine proof of Theorem 1.1. The energy balance is a discrete model, not an independently proved continuum energy estimate.

Published result: The reference construction’s Introduction (citing Craik–Criminale [9], exact finite-amplitude waves on affine background flows) and Section 2.2’s description of the pulses: the background shear supplies growth, shortening the radial wavelength raises viscous damping, amplification dominates first and damping later. The program makes the Craik–Criminale wavevector law exact for simple shear and bisects the amplification/damping crossover of a representative growth-rate model to an exact rational bracket.

References:

  • OpenAI, “Finite time blowup for Navier–Stokes” (2026; the PDF carries no date line, the year is the one the program headers give). Source: mathematics_stacks_nonabelian_descent.esk. SHA-256: ec081828506dfeb2f49624d1dc0d6433da10330f60ae1e7d9a0690b00833d097.

Published result: G-torsors on a space are classified by nonabelian H¹, i.e. Hom(π₁, G)/G with automorphisms the centralizers (Giraud), and the torsor stack satisfies descent along covers whose intersections are contractible (Hollander; Lurie 6.5.3–6.5.4). The program evaluates the state sums exactly in cyclotomic fields.

Crossed-module nerves and Postnikov data

Source: mathematics_two_groups_postnikov.esk. SHA-256: 506ec63d21f893faf59f35ed1e17a65ecb2faf48d1a601ef00bc150b0a8c0f62.

Published result: Strict 2-groups are crossed modules (Whitehead 1949); the classifying space of a crossed module d: M → N is a 2-type with π₁ = coker d and π₂ = ker d (Brown–Higgins–Sivera §2.5), classified by π₁, π₂ and a k-invariant in H³(π₁; π₂) (Baez–Lauda §8), with Z/4 → Z/4 (sign action) realizing the nontrivial class for π₁ = π₂ = Z/2. The program enumerates the nerves (Duskin’s description) and shows that cohomology in degree 2 separates 2-types with equal homotopy groups.

References:

  • J. H. C. Whitehead, “Combinatorial homotopy II”, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 55 (1949). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • R. Brown, P. J. Higgins, R. Sivera, Nonabelian Algebraic Topology, EMS (2011). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. Duskin, “Simplicial matrices and the nerves of weak n-categories I”, Theory Appl. Categ. 9 (2002). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. C. Baez, A. D. Lauda, “Higher-dimensional algebra V: 2-groups”, Theory Appl. Categ. 12 (2004). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. P. May, Simplicial Objects in Algebraic Topology (1967), §23. (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Distinguish 2-types with identical π₁ and π₂ using k-sensitive cohomology.

Implemented algorithm: Check crossed-module/Peiffer laws, enumerate edge/triangle-labeled nerve simplices, check face identities and compute integral/mod-2 complexes.

Domain and parameters: Finite abelian crossed modules including Z/2→1,1→Z/2,Z/2→Z/2 and Z/4→Z/4 with trivial/sign action; source-defined low degrees.

Arithmetic: Exact integer and finite-field linear algebra.

Checks in the source: Kernel/cokernel homotopy sizes, cohomology dimensions, nontrivial-twist distinction and dropped-tetrahedron-equation negative controls are asserted.

Limits: Finite-degree computations distinguish these presentations; equivalence of entire 2-types invokes the cited crossed-module/Postnikov theory.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.

Yetter invariants on the 64-point torus

Source: mathematics_yetter_three_torus_finite_model.esk. SHA-256: 3378acb1aa13827bc82f111bfd7a07049f902cf4115d09cf8f50866a2c702b75.

Published result: Yetter’s 2-group invariants are topological, so on any triangulation of T³ they must equal the values computed on the one-vertex six-tetrahedron triangulation in the sibling program. The program recomputes nine of them on the 384-tetrahedron order complex of the 64-point finite model of T³ (McCord), where brute-force enumeration (|N|^385 labellings) is out of reach and the 1-gauge reduction is used, and checks them against the Postnikov fibration formula.

References:

  • D. N. Yetter, “TQFT’s from homotopy 2-types”, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 2 (1993). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • T. Porter, “Topological quantum field theories from homotopy n-types”, J. London Math. Soc. 58 (1998). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. Faria Martins, T. Porter, “On Yetter’s invariant and an extension of the Dijkgraaf-Witten invariant to categorical groups”, Theory Appl. Categ. 18 (2007). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • M. C. McCord, “Singular homology groups and homotopy groups of finite topological spaces”, Duke Math. J. 33 (1966). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. A. Barmak, Algebraic Topology of Finite Topological Spaces and Applications, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 2032, Springer (2011). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Recompute 2-group invariants on a larger finite-space triangulation.

Implemented algorithm: Use spanning-tree holonomies, 1-gauge reduction, cached twisted Smith forms and independent fibration counts.

Domain and parameters: 64 vertices/448 edges/768 triangles/384 tetrahedra; nine supplied crossed modules; 8 or 27 holonomies.

Arithmetic: Exact integer/modular Smith forms and rational normalizations, including denominator factors 2³⁸⁴ or 3³⁸⁴.

Checks in the source: The nine stated invariants and two routes agree exactly; source checks twelve reused Smith forms and twisted-coefficient orders.

Limits: Avoids impossible brute-force edge enumeration using a source-derived gauge reduction; the reduction is checked against full enumeration in the sibling lens-space program, not here. The measured outcome below records the run time at the release SHA; the program’s own wall-time and peak-memory report goes to the compiler measurement stream, not to this catalogue.

Yetter state sums and Postnikov fibration

Source: mathematics_yetter_two_group_invariants.esk. SHA-256: 51777e8a49ad8535dea26ca65a9bc8c10f262fc287146a89087f5177720a065f.

Published result: Yetter (1993) defines a 3-manifold invariant from a finite 2-group as a normalized count of simplicial maps into the nerve of the 2-group; Faria Martins and Porter (2007) identify it with the homotopy cardinality of the mapping space Map(X, BG), computable through the Postnikov fibration K(π₂, 2) → BG → Bπ₁ with the k-invariant as an obstruction and local coefficients twisted by π₁. The program computes both routes for six crossed modules on S³, RP³ and T³.

References:

  • D. N. Yetter, “TQFT’s from homotopy 2-types”, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 2 (1993). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • T. Porter, “Topological quantum field theories from homotopy n-types”, J. London Math. Soc. 58 (1998). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. Faria Martins, T. Porter, “On Yetter’s invariant and an extension of the Dijkgraaf-Witten invariant to categorical groups”, Theory Appl. Categ. 18 (2007). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. C. Baez, J. Dolan, “From finite sets to Feynman diagrams” (2001). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • J. C. Baez, A. D. Lauda, “Higher-dimensional algebra V: 2-groups”, Theory Appl. Categ. 12 (2004). (as cited in the program’s source comments)
  • A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press (2002). (as cited in the program’s source comments)

Purpose: Compare explicit crossed-module state sums with mapping-space formulas.

Implemented algorithm: Gauge-fix edge labels, solve affine triangle equations by Smith forms and evaluate local-coefficient obstruction/fibration counts.

Domain and parameters: Supplied S³,RP³,T³ Delta-complexes and six crossed modules, including sign-action Z/4→Z/4 and Z/3→Z/2.

Arithmetic: Exact group labels, integer Smith forms and rational cardinalities.

Checks in the source: Presentation-equivalence cases, RP³ k-obstruction, twisted coefficient orders and independent counting-route equality are asserted.

Limits: Counts apply to these finite complexes/modules; general topological invariance and mapping-space interpretations use cited theorems.

Prerequisites: Built eshkol-run and stdlib; native JIT or AOT.
